key_terms.meaning: E = hν = hc/λ, where h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, ν = frequency in Hz (s⁻¹), λ = wavelength in m, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹
ν̄ = 1/λ, the number of waves per cm when λ is in cm; unit cm⁻¹, used for IR and microwave spectra
A = log₁₀(I₀/I), where I₀ = intensity of light entering the sample and I = intensity leaving it; a pure number, no units
ε in A = εcl, where c = concentration in mol L⁻¹ and l = path length in cm; unit L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹
The part of a molecule that absorbs UV-visible light, usually a conjugated π system or a group with lone pairs such as C=O or N=N
A saturated group with lone pairs (–OH, –NH₂, –Cl) attached to a chromophore; it shifts absorption to longer wavelength and raises intensity
Movement of an absorption maximum to a longer wavelength, caused by extra conjugation or by an auxochrome
Energy difference between the highest occupied and lowest unoccupied molecular orbitals; UV-visible absorption of lowest energy equals this gap
A coordinated motion of nuclei in which all atoms move at the same frequency, such as symmetric stretch, asymmetric stretch or bending
ν̄ = (1/2πc)√(k/μ), where k = force constant in N m⁻¹ and μ = reduced mass in kg; stronger bonds and lighter atoms absorb at higher wavenumber
A narrow wavenumber range in which a particular functional group always absorbs, for example C=O near 1700 cm⁻¹
B = h/(8π²Ic), where I = moment of inertia in kg m²; expressed in cm⁻¹, it fixes the spacing of rotational lines
Only ΔJ = ±1 is allowed for a linear rotor with a permanent dipole, so successive absorption lines are spaced 2B apart
δ = (ν_sample − ν_reference)/ν_reference × 10⁶, quoted in ppm relative to tetramethylsilane (TMS); it measures the shielding of a nucleus
A proton next to n equivalent protons appears as n+1 lines because the neighbouring nuclear spins give n+1 different local fields
Because nuclei are at least ~1836 times heavier than an electron, nuclear and electronic motions are treated separately
An electronic transition is so fast that nuclei do not move during it; the transition is drawn as a vertical line on a potential-energy diagram
Φ = (number of molecules of product formed) ÷ (number of photons absorbed); also called the quantum efficiency
Emission from an excited singlet state back to the ground state, with the same spin multiplicity; lifetime is roughly 10⁻⁹ to 10⁻⁷ s
Emission from the lowest triplet state after intersystem crossing; spin-forbidden, so the lifetime is 10⁻³ s to seconds or longer

takeaways: A molecule absorbs light only when the photon energy hν matches the gap between two of its own energy levels, so each technique sees a different kind of gap.
Beer–Lambert makes colour measurement quantitative: absorbance is a straight-line function of concentration, which is why colorimeters work.
In UV-visible spectroscopy the gap is electronic, so conjugation and chromophores decide both the wavelength and how strongly the sample absorbs.
IR spectroscopy reports vibrations, so functional groups can be read off a spectrum in their characteristic wavenumber ranges.
Microwave lines of a rigid rotor are equally spaced by 2B, which turns a spectrum into a moment of inertia and then a bond length.
NMR converts chemical environment into chemical shift and the number of neighbours into splitting, giving a map of the carbon skeleton and its hydrogens.
Born–Oppenheimer and Franck–Condon together explain why electronic bands are broad and carry vibrational structure.
Photochemistry begins only after a photon is absorbed, and quantum yield tells you how many product molecules one absorbed photon actually delivers.
The Jablonski diagram sorts out the competing fates of an excited molecule and explains why phosphorescence is slow and long-lived.
bank_note: Long answers usually combine a labelled diagram (potential-energy curves, Jablonski diagram, or an NMR/IR spectrum) with the defining equation and then move to an application or a numerical problem, so practise the derivations and the calculations together.

bank.q: State the Beer–Lambert law, define absorbance and transmittance, and derive the relation A = εcl. List three situations in which the law fails for a real solution.
outline: Statement: A = log₁₀(I₀/I) = εcl with each symbol defined and units given
Derivation from the fraction of light absorbed by successive thin layers of solution
Absorbance is additive while transmittance is multiplicative

Failures: high concentration (solute interaction), stray light or polychromatic radiation, scattering or turbidity, chemical shift of the absorbing species with concentration, fluorescence in the sample

bank.q: Explain what a chromophore is and why increasing conjugation shifts the absorption maximum to a longer wavelength. Illustrate with ethene, butadiene and benzene.
outline: Chromophore definition, with σ → σ*, n → π* and π → π* transitions named and ordered by energy
Longer conjugated chain means the π electrons are delocalised over more centres, so the HOMO–LUMO gap shrinks
Ethene absorbs far in the UV, butadiene near 217 nm, benzene with its own characteristic bands
Auxochromes and their red shift and hyperchromic effect mentioned
Woodward–Fieser type reasoning may be added if the syllabus covers it

bank.q: Describe the vibrational modes of a linear triatomic molecule and state the conditions a vibration must satisfy to be infrared active. Explain why CO₂ shows two stretching bands but not the symmetric one.
outline: Degrees of freedom: 3N − 5 for linear, 3N − 6 for non-linear, with numbers worked out
Symmetric stretch, asymmetric stretch, two degenerate bends named and sketched
Infrared activity requires a change in dipole moment during the vibration
CO₂ symmetric stretch gives no dipole change, hence IR inactive; asymmetric stretch and bend are active
Absorption positions linked to force constant and reduced mass

bank.q: Explain chemical shift and spin–spin splitting in proton NMR. Why is tetramethylsilane used as the reference, and what does the n+1 rule predict?
outline: Nuclear spin of ¹H is ½, giving two orientations in an applied field B₀
Electron cloud shields the nucleus, so each chemically distinct proton resonates at a slightly different frequency
δ in ppm defined, TMS chosen because it is inert, volatile, soluble, gives one sharp signal and absorbs upfield of most protons
n+1 rule explained through the n+1 possible sums of neighbouring spin states
Pascal-triangle intensities and the need for equivalent neighbours

bank.q: State the Born–Oppenheimer approximation and the Franck–Condon principle. Use them to explain why an electronic absorption band has vibrational fine structure.
outline: Nuclear mass far exceeds electron mass, so electronic and nuclear motions are separable
Electronic energies computed for fixed nuclei give potential-energy curves
Electronic transition is vertical because nuclei cannot move in about 10⁻¹⁵ s
Franck–Condon factor as the square of the overlap of the vibrational wavefunctions
Several vibrational levels of the upper state reached, so a band system with fine structure appears
Explain why the 0–0 band is not always the strongest line

bank.q: State the two laws of photochemistry and define quantum yield. Give reasons why a quantum yield can be much greater than one or much less than one.
outline: Grotthuss–Draper law: only absorbed light brings about chemical change
Stark–Einstein law: one photon is absorbed per molecule activated in the primary step
Φ defined as product molecules per photon absorbed, and overall versus primary quantum yield distinguished
Φ > 1 through chain reactions, for example H₂ + Cl₂
Φ < 1 through de-excitation by fluorescence, quenching, internal conversion or recombination
Numerical example showing Φ calculated from amount of product and light absorbed

bank.q: Draw and explain the Jablonski diagram. Distinguish fluorescence from phosphorescence in terms of spin states, lifetimes and conditions of observation.
outline: Absorption, internal conversion, vibrational relaxation, intersystem crossing, fluorescence and phosphorescence placed correctly
Singlet and triplet states with multiplicity explained
Fluorescence: same multiplicity, allowed, 10⁻⁹ to 10⁻⁷ s, seen at room temperature
Phosphorescence: requires intersystem crossing, spin-forbidden, long lived, usually seen in rigid or frozen media
Kasha's rule and Stokes shift mentioned

bank.q: A coloured solution in a 1.00 cm cell shows absorbance 0.70 at 510 nm. Its molar absorptivity there is 1.4 × 10⁴ L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹. Calculate the concentration, and then the absorbance if the same solution were measured in a 2.50 cm cell.
outline: Use c = A/(εl)
New absorbance scales linearly with path length: A = 0.70 × 2.50 = 1.75
Comment that absorbance above about 1.5 is unreliable on simple instruments

bank.q: The first two pure rotational absorption lines of a diatomic molecule lie at 3.84 cm⁻¹ and 7.68 cm⁻¹. Find the rotational constant B, the moment of inertia, and outline how the bond length is obtained.
outline: Lines for J = 0 → 1 and J = 1 → 2 occur at 2B and 4B, so spacing 2B = 3.84 cm⁻¹
B = 1.92 cm⁻¹
Convert B to m⁻¹ and use I = h/(8π²Bc)
Reduced mass from atomic masses, then r = √(I/μ)
State the rigid rotor assumptions and the ΔJ = ±1 selection rule

bank.q: A nanostructured ZnO film shows a sharp rise in absorption below 380 nm. Estimate its optical bandgap in eV and state which electronic transition the light is driving.
outline: E = hc/λ = 1240/λ(nm) eV
Transition is valence band to conduction band across the bandgap
The absorption edge is used as the measurement point; Tauc-type extrapolation may be mentioned for accuracy

bank.q: A compound of molecular formula C₃H₆O shows a strong IR band at 1715 cm⁻¹, no UV absorption above 300 nm, and a single sharp NMR line at δ ≈ 2.1 ppm. Identify the compound and justify each observation.
outline: 1715 cm⁻¹ fits a non-conjugated C=O stretch
No UV absorption above 300 nm means no conjugated chromophore
A single NMR line means all six hydrogens are equivalent
Acetone (propan-2-one) satisfies all three
Contrast with propanal, which would show an aldehydic proton near δ 9–10 and a second IR band

bank.q: Describe how you would determine the concentration of an unknown potassium permanganate solution with a colorimeter. Give the steps, the working equation and four precautions.
outline: Prepare a blank and a set of standard solutions by dilution
Choose a filter or wavelength at the absorption maximum, here the green region near 525 nm
Measure absorbance of standards and plot A against c; the plot should be a straight line through the origin
Read the unknown's absorbance and find c from the calibration graph
Precautions: same cell and orientation, no bubbles, absorbance kept between 0.1 and 1.0, fresh standards, clean optics, monochromatic light

bank.q: Compare UV-visible, infrared and NMR spectroscopy as tools for identifying an unknown organic liquid. What information does each supply, and in what order would you use them?
outline: UV-visible gives conjugation and chromophore information but cannot identify a full structure
IR gives the functional groups present, and the fingerprint region helps confirm identity
NMR gives the hydrogen count, environments and connectivities
Order of use: IR and NMR first for structure, UV-visible for conjugation and for quantitative assay
Limitations named: UV-visible is insensitive to saturated molecules, IR is poor for symmetry-forbidden modes, NMR needs deuterated solvents

bank.q: A photochemical reaction has a measured overall quantum yield of 0.02. Explain what this value means, suggest the competing de-excitation pathways, and judge whether the process is industrially attractive.
outline: Φ defined in terms of product molecules per photon absorbed
Low Φ means most excited molecules return to the ground state without reaction
Competing pathways: fluorescence, internal conversion, intersystem crossing, quenching by oxygen or solvent, cage recombination
Industrial judgement: low photon efficiency means high lamp power cost per kilogram of product; would need a chain reaction or a cheaper light source
Compare with a chain reaction where Φ may reach 10⁴ to 10⁶

bank.q: Phosphorescence is observed from a dilute solution frozen at 77 K but not from the same solution at room temperature. Explain this using the Jablonski diagram and rate constants, and comment on why triplet emission is long-lived.
outline: Intersystem crossing from S₁ to T₁ competes with fluorescence
T₁ to S₀ emission is spin-forbidden, so the radiative rate constant is small and the lifetime is long
At room temperature collisions, oxygen quenching and solvent motions deactivate the triplet non-radiatively
In a rigid glass at 77 K diffusion stops, so non-radiative decay is suppressed and phosphorescence survives
Practical consequence: phosphorescent probes and glow-in-the-dark materials need a rigid host

glossary.def: The study of how matter absorbs or emits electromagnetic radiation, used to deduce structure and measure concentration.
The full range of radiation from gamma rays to radio waves, all travelling at c in vacuum and differing only in frequency.
Number of wave cycles passing a point per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
Distance between two successive crests of a wave, usually in nm for UV-visible and in μm or cm⁻¹ for infrared.
The fraction T = I/I₀ of incident light that passes through the sample, often quoted as a percentage.
A plot of absorbance against known concentration, used to read off an unknown concentration.
An instrument that compares the colour intensity of a solution with a standard using a fixed wavelength filter.
An instrument that measures absorbance as a function of wavelength using a monochromator or grating.
The absorbance of a 1 mol L⁻¹ solution in a 1 cm cell; a measure of how strongly a species absorbs at a given wavelength.
A move of the absorption maximum to longer wavelength and lower energy, usually due to conjugation or an auxochrome.
Excitation of an electron from a bonding π orbital to an antibonding π* orbital, typically strong and in the UV region.
Excitation of a lone-pair electron to a π* orbital; weak and at longer wavelength than π → π*.
The 1400–600 cm⁻¹ part of an IR spectrum, rich in coupled modes and useful for confirming identity.
μ = m₁m₂/(m₁ + m₂), the effective mass used in the vibration and rotation of a diatomic molecule.
The number of independent ways a molecule can move; 3N total, giving 3N − 6 vibrational modes for a non-linear molecule.
I = μr² for a diatomic molecule, with r the bond length; it fixes the rotational energy levels.
Shielding of a nucleus that depends on orientation, as in aromatic rings where ring current shifts protons downfield.
A larger chemical shift (higher δ), meaning the nucleus is less shielded and resonates at higher frequency.
A non-radiative change of spin state, for example from an excited singlet to a triplet.
A non-radiative transition between electronic states of the same spin multiplicity.
The energy difference between the absorption and emission maxima, caused by vibrational relaxation in the excited state.
Loss of excitation energy through collision or energy transfer to another molecule, reducing emission intensity.
A self-propagating sequence of steps in which one photon produces many product molecules, giving quantum yield above one.
